title: Sliding-window VWAP
text: One more interview classic. Compute the volume weighted average price of the last N seconds of trades, and update it on every trade. VWAP is the sum of price times quantity, divided by total quantity. Use exchange time, and stay exact.

title: The first answer
text: The first answer keeps the window in a deque. Push each trade on the back, pop expired trades off the front, then loop over the whole window to sum it again. That is linear in the trades per window. A busy stock can print thousands of trades in a second, so every update walks thousands of entries.

title: Running sums
text: Instead, keep two running sums: price times quantity, and quantity. A new trade adds to both. An expiring trade subtracts from both. The VWAP is then one division. Every trade is added once and removed once, so an update is O(1) amortized.

title: Fixed ring
text: Store the window in a fixed capacity ring. Its size is a power of two, so an index wraps with a mask. Head and tail are 64 bit counters that only grow. Evict from the front while the oldest trade is at or before now minus the window. If the ring is full, reject the trade loudly, rather than drop a live one.

title: Exact integers
text: Prices stay in Price(4), as integers. One trade's price times quantity can approach two to the 64. So the sum of products lives in an unsigned 128 bit integer. A plain 64 bit sum can wrap on the second such trade. The result rounds half up, back to Price(4).

title: Exchange time
text: The window runs on exchange timestamps, the nanoseconds in each ITCH message, not the local clock. A replay then gives the same answer as live, and our own queueing delay cannot change the window. A timestamp that goes backwards is rejected. If no trades arrive, call evict from a timer.

title: Moving max and min
text: The same window also gives a moving high and low, with a monotonic deque. Before pushing a trade, pop every back entry priced at or below it. The front is then the maximum. Expire the front on time, just like the ring. Each trade is pushed and popped at most once, so this is O(1) amortized too.

title: Tests and complexity
text: The tests cover an empty window, equal timestamps, the exact boundary, time going backwards, a full ring, rounding, and maximal trades. Then 300 thousand random trades, with bursts and quiet gaps, are checked against the naive deque after every one. Memory is fixed at the ring's capacity.

title: Benchmark
text: Timing it on a shared four vCPU cloud box, busy with other jobs, with a one second window. With a thousand trades in the window, the naive deque took 3 to 4 microseconds per trade. With ten thousand, 26 to 36. The ring took 73 to 125 nanoseconds in both cases, including the 128 bit divide and the high and low.
